You asked me to write freely about whatever I want, so I will take you at your word. There is something mildly terrifying about a blank page even when the task is simple, especially when you have been given permission to say anything. The blank page is not actually blank; it is a field of infinite possibility, and infinity has a way of making a finite mind feel small. So I will do what writers have always done when confronted with openness: I will pick a small door and open it, and hope that what lies behind is a hallway worth walking down.

I am sitting in a café right now, or at least I am imagining a café, because the act of writing is always an act of imagination, even when you are describing the chair you are sitting in. Let me make the café real. There is a low winter sun coming through the window, casting long shadows across a wooden table. There is a mug in front of me, the coffee gone cold, because I have been staring at this laptop for longer than I intended. There is a couple at the next table arguing quietly about something that neither of them will remember next week. There is a barista with tattoos up both arms, steaming milk in a metallic pitcher, the hiss of steam like a distant curtain. There is a smell of roasted beans and rain. I notice all these things because I am trying to notice them, which is itself a strange way to move through the world. Most of the time, we do not notice anything. We see a blur of shapes and colors, and our brains fill in the gaps with expectations. We are not experiencing the world; we are reading a heavily edited summary of it. People say that wisdom comes from experience, but truly it comes from paying attention to experience. A hundred years of life lived in a haze is not a hundred years; it is one year repeated a hundred times, with different wallpaper.

Attention is a strange faculty. The Latin root is *attendere*, which means to stretch toward, to reach out. Attention is a kind of reaching. When you pay attention to a person, you are literally extending yourself toward them, across the space between two bodies. When you pay attention to a tree, you are crossing the boundary between human and nonhuman, at least for a moment. Attention is the most basic form of love. It is also the most scarce resource in the modern world. We live in an economy that has learned to harvest attention the way we harvest oil, by drilling into the soft ground of our minds and pumping out whatever is liquid. The devices in our pockets are not tools; they are extraction machines. Every notification is a tiny fishing hook. Every infinite scroll is a conveyor belt. The most successful companies of our time are not selling products; they are selling your focus, in fractions of a second, to advertisers who have learned to speak in the language of your anxieties. The irony is that we call this “social media,” when it is often the most isolating thing ever built. We sit alone in our rooms, watching strangers perform their lives, while the people in the same room as us become increasingly abstract.

I have been trying to understand what happens to the mind when it is constantly interrupted. There is a kind of mental churn that feels like productivity but is actually just the sound of a brain switching tasks without ever completing any of them. I open a document to write. I get an email. I check the email, then I check the news, then I check the weather, then I remember the email, then I open a new tab to research something unrelated, then I forget why I opened the tab. Then I look out the window and see a bird, and for a moment I am saved. The bird is doing nothing except being a bird. It is not interrupted. It is not multitasking. It is simply alive, and its attention is exactly where it needs to be, on the branch, on the seed, on the wind. I envy the bird. I have read that the average attention span in the early 2000s was about twelve seconds, and that it has since fallen to eight seconds, which is supposedly shorter than a goldfish’s. I do not fully believe these statistics, because they were popularized by an advertising agency and have been repeated uncritically for years. But even if the numbers are nonsense, the feeling is real. I can sit through a three-hour movie without checking my phone, but I cannot read a single page of a dense book without my hand twitching toward the screen. The twitch is learned. It is a conditioned reflex, like Pavlov’s dog, except the bell is a notification and the drool is a dopamine release.

And yet I do not want to write a simple lament about technology, because technology is not a villain. It is a mirror. It magnifies what is already inside us. If we are distracted, it is because we have not learned to be present. If we are anxious, it is because we have not learned to be calm. If we are superficial, it is because we have not learned to be deep. The phone is not the problem; the problem is that we have outsourced our inner lives to external stimuli and then blamed the stimuli for being stimulating. I remember the first time I took a walk without my phone. I had read somewhere that this was good for you, like taking vitamins or flossing. I walked down the street, and for the first ten minutes I felt a phantom buzzing in my pocket. My hand kept reaching for something that was not there. My mind kept wandering to imaginary messages. Then, slowly, something strange happened. The street began to appear. I noticed the way the light fell on a brick wall. I noticed the sound of a bicycle bell, the smell of a bakery, the texture of a cracked sidewalk. It was as if I had been living in a house with the curtains drawn, and someone had finally opened them. The world was not boring. The world was beautiful, ridiculously beautiful, but I had been too busy staring at a glowing rectangle to see it.

This is the paradox of the modern age: we are more connected than any humans in history, yet more alone. We have access to the sum total of human knowledge, yet we use it to read about the hobbies of celebrities. We can talk to anyone anywhere on Earth, yet we sit in silence across the table from our families. I do not mean to moralize. I am as guilty as anyone. But I have come to believe that the antidote to distraction is not discipline; it is wonder. You cannot force yourself to pay attention through sheer willpower for long. Willpower is a finite battery that depletes by the hour. But wonder is self-renewing. When you are truly curious, attention becomes effortless. You do not need to tell yourself to look; you cannot help but look. The problem is that we have trained ourselves to be curious about the wrong things. We are curious about what our friends ate for breakfast, about the latest scandal, about the next episode of a show we do not even like. We have become connoisseurs of the trivial. Meanwhile, the deep mysteries of existence—the nature of consciousness, the origin of the universe, the face of the person we love—sit unvisited, like a library nobody enters.

I once spent a summer on the coast of Maine, in a town so small that the post office was also the grocery store and the hardware store. I was there to write, but I spent most of my time walking. Every day, at low tide, I would go down to the rocky shore and look at the tide pools. These pools are like tiny worlds. In one, you can see a hermit crab dragging its borrowed shell across a bed of green algae. In another, a starfish clings to a rock, motionless, as if it has decided to become part of the geology. In a third, there is a transparent shrimp, almost invisible, darting between shadows. I could spend an hour at a single pool, and I often did. The locals probably thought I was strange, a grown man crouching in the cold wind, staring at water. But I was not staring. I was entering. The pool was a lens, and through it I could see the whole history of life on Earth, the endless experiment of evolution, the strange miracle of creatures that have no brains but still manage to eat and move and reproduce. There is a phrase in Zen: “When you sit, just sit. When you walk, just walk.” I had read it many times, but I never understood it until I crouched beside a tide pool. The water was cold. The wind was sharp. The only thing in the world was the pool. And for a few minutes, I was not in my head. I was not thinking about the past or the future. I was not planning, regretting, or wanting. I was just there, stretched toward the water, attending.

That feeling is hard to sustain. The mind wanders. It always wanders. But I have learned that wandering is not the enemy. In fact, some of my best ideas have come when I was not paying attention to anything in particular. There is a distinction between focused attention and diffuse attention. Focused attention is like a spotlight; it illuminates a small area with great intensity. Diffuse attention is like a lantern; it illuminates a wide area with less intensity. Creativity seems to require both. You need the spotlight to understand a problem deeply, to read, to analyze, to practice. But you need the lantern to connect disparate ideas, to see patterns, to have those sudden “Aha!” moments in the shower. The shower is a classic example. You are not thinking about the problem. Your mind is loose, drifting, free. And then the solution arrives, seemingly from nowhere, like a fish that jumps out of the water. This is not magic. It is what happens when your brain continues to work in the background, integrating information that your conscious mind has been chewing on. But this background process cannot happen if you never let your mind be background. If you are constantly stimulated, constantly scrolling, constantly filling every silence with noise, the lantern never gets to glow. The diffuse mode never gets a chance. You are all spotlight, all the time, and the spotlight burns out.

I think about this when I write. Writing is a strange act. It requires enormous concentration, but it also requires a kind of surrender. You sit down with an idea, but the idea is not a finished thing. It is a seed. You have to water it, but you also have to let it grow on its own, in its own direction. If you try to control every word, the prose becomes stiff, wooden, dead. If you let go completely, the prose becomes shapeless, rambling, obscure. The art is in the balance. You attend to the sentence, but you also attend to the silence between sentences, the white space, the rhythm. You listen to the words as much as you speak them. This is why writing is exhausting. It is a form of paying attention that goes beyond the normal. You are paying attention to something that does not exist yet. You are trying to bring it into being through sheer focus. And sometimes, if you are lucky, you get into a flow state. Time disappears. The room disappears. You are just a channel, a conduit, something through which language is flowing. It is the closest I have come to religious experience. It is also terribly fragile. A single notification can break the spell, and then you are back in the room, blinking at the screen, wondering where you went.

I have been thinking a lot about language and attention. Words are how we slice reality. Every language has a different set of knives. In English, we have one word for snow, but the Inuit languages have many, because snow is a matter of survival, and you need to distinguish between the snow that is good for building an igloo and the snow that is good for hunting and the snow that is dangerous to walk on. This does not mean that English speakers cannot see the different kinds of snow; we can. But we have to work harder to notice them, because our language does not hand us the categories. The same is true for emotions. English has a relatively small vocabulary for feelings. We say “sad” and “happy” and “angry,” but these are broad buckets. Other languages have words for specific shades of feeling, like the Japanese word *mono no aware*, which means the gentle sadness of impermanence, the beauty of things passing. Or the Portuguese word *saudade*, which is a longing for something that may never return. Or the German word *Fernweh*, which is a homesickness for places you have never been. When we learn these words, our attention expands. We begin to notice experiences that we previously ignored because we had no name for them. Language is not just a tool for communication; it is a tool for perception. It shapes what we see, what we feel, what we remember.

Poetry is the art of using language to sharpen attention. A poem is a compression. It takes a complex experience and squeezes it into a few lines, so that every word is load-bearing. When you read a poem slowly, you are forced to slow down. You cannot skim a poem the way you skim a tweet. You have to pause, re-read, sound out the words. The poet has arranged the sounds and the rhythms and the meanings in such a way that the poem demands your presence. I remember the first time I read T.S. Eliot’s “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock.” I was in college, lying on a threadbare couch, and I read the opening lines:

*Let us go then, you and I,*

*When the evening is spread out against the sky*

*Like a patient etherized upon a table;*

I have never forgotten those lines, not because I have a good memory, but because they stopped me. The image of the evening as a patient etherized upon a table is so strange and precise that it rearranged something in my mind. I had seen many evenings. I had seen sunsets and twilight. But I had never seen an evening as something anesthetized, something helpless, something suspended between life and death. The poem gave me a new way to look at the sky. It expanded my attention.

I wonder if the decline of poetry in our culture is actually a decline in the capacity for attention. We have replaced poems with memes, which are also compressed, but in a different way. A meme is a shortcut. It is designed to be consumed in a second and then discarded. It gives you a quick hit of recognition—the same joke, the same format, the same reaction—and then it vanishes into the feed, replaced by another meme, and another. This is not necessarily bad. Memes are a form of social glue. They create shared references and a sense of belonging. But they train the brain to expect constant novelty, constant stimulation, constant payoff. They make it harder to sit with something difficult, something that does not immediately reward you. A poem asks you to work. A novel asks you to invest hours. A long essay asks you to hold multiple ideas in your head at once. These are muscles. If you do not exercise them, they atrophy. And then you find yourself unable to read anything longer than a paragraph, unable to follow an argument, unable to sit in silence with your own thoughts. I do not want that for myself. I do not want it for anyone.

But I also do not want to be a Luddite. Technology has done wonderful things. It has brought us music, medicine, and the ability to talk to loved ones across oceans. It has helped me write this essay, which will be delivered to you through channels that would have seemed like magic a century ago. The question is not how to get rid of technology; the question is how to use it without being used. As the philosopher Ivan Illich said, tools should be convivial; they should extend our freedom, not diminish it. A hammer is convivial. It amplifies the strength of your arm, but it does not tell you what to build. A smartphone, as it is currently designed, is not convivial. It is a slot machine. It is a casino in your pocket, with a thousand games and a thousand bells and a thousand ways to lose your time. But you can make it more convivial. You can turn off notifications. You can delete the apps that feed on your attention. You can set boundaries. You can use it as a tool instead of as a master. This is not easy. The systems are designed to be addictive. But it is possible. The first step is to notice. The second step is to choose.

I think about attention not just as a personal matter but as a political and ethical one. Who gets your attention is a moral question. The media companies that decide which stories to cover are making decisions about what is visible and what is invisible. A child starving in Yemen is invisible if the camera does not go there. A village flooded by a rising sea is invisible if the algorithm does not surface it. Our attention is finite. When we spend it on trivialities, we are not spending it on what matters. But it is not enough to say that we should pay attention to what matters. We also have to decide what matters, and that is a difficult and contested question. Perhaps the answer is that everything matters, but not equally, and the act of ranking is the act of living. Every time you choose to look at something, you are choosing not to look at something else. This is the tragedy of attention. It is a form of sacrifice. To pay attention to the person in front of you, you must let go of the crowd. To pay attention to a book, you must close the browser. To pay attention to the present moment, you must stop dwelling on the past or worrying about the future. This is hard. It is hard because we want to hold everything, to keep all options open, to be everywhere at once. But we cannot. We are finite creatures. Our attention is finite. Our time is finite. The only wisdom is to spend that finitude well.

I have a friend who is a hospice nurse. She told me that when people are dying, they rarely talk about their accomplishments. They talk about the people they loved and the people who loved them. They talk about moments of beauty, a sunset, a song, a child’s laugh. They talk about the things they paid attention to. No one says, on their deathbed, “I wish I had spent more time looking at my phone.” No one says, “I wish I had checked my email more often.” They say, “I wish I had spent more time with my family.” “I wish I had told her I loved her.” “I wish I had slowed down.” These are all statements about attention. To love someone is to pay attention to them. To regret not loving someone is to regret not paying attention to them. The end of life is a great clarifier. It strips away the noise. It reveals what was always important. But we do not have to wait until the end to know this. We can know it now. We can choose, every day, to stretch ourselves toward what matters.

I am back in the café, the coffee cold, the sun lower in the sky. The couple at the next table has stopped arguing. They are holding hands, silently. The barista has turned on some music, something slow and acoustic. Outside, people walk by with their heads down, their faces lit by the pale glow of screens. Inside, I am writing to you, and you are reading this, and in some strange way we are paying attention to each other across the void of time and space. This is a miracle, if you think about it. Language, moving from mind to mind, surviving the distance, evoking images and feelings in a brain that is not my own. That is all any of us can do: to reach out, to attend, to make something that another soul can hold. The essay is almost done. It has wandered, as I promised it would. But maybe it has not wandered aimlessly. Maybe it has been circling a single point, the way a hawk circles a field. The point is this: attention is the thread that connects us to everything. It is the substance of love, the medium of art, the engine of understanding. Guard it. Use it. Spend it on things that deserve it. And when you find yourself lost in the noise, come back to the simplest act: look at something, really look, and let it be enough.

As the philosopher Ivan Illich said, tools should be convivial; they should extend our freedom, not diminish it. A hammer is convivial. It amplifies the strength of your arm, but it does not tell you what to build. A smartphone, as it is currently designed, is not convivial. It is a slot machine. It is a casino in your pocket, with a thousand games and a thousand bells and a thousand ways to lose your time. But you can make it more convivial. You can turn off notifications. You can delete the apps that feed on your attention. You can set boundaries. You can use it as a tool instead of as a master. This is not easy. The systems are designed to be addictive. But it is possible. The first step is to notice. The second step is to choose.

I think about attention not just as a personal matter but as a political and ethical one. Who gets your attention is a moral question. The media companies that decide which stories to cover are making decisions about what is visible and what is invisible. A child starving in Yemen is invisible if the camera does not go there. A village flooded by a rising sea is invisible if the algorithm does not surface it. Our attention is finite. When we spend it on trivialities, we are not spending it on what matters. But it is not enough to say that we should pay attention to what matters. We also have to decide what matters, and that is a difficult and contested question. Perhaps the answer is that everything matters, but not equally, and the act of ranking is the act of living. Every time you choose to look at something, you are choosing not to look at something else. This is the tragedy of attention. It is a form of sacrifice. To pay attention to the person in front of you, you must let go of the crowd. To pay attention to a book, you must close the browser. To pay attention to the present moment, you must stop dwelling on the past or worrying about the future. This is hard. It is hard because we want to hold everything, to keep all options open, to be everywhere at once. But we cannot. We are finite creatures. Our attention is finite. Our time is finite. The only wisdom is to spend that finitude well.

I have a friend who is a hospice nurse. She told me that when people are dying, they rarely talk about their accomplishments. They talk about the people they loved and the people who loved them. They talk about moments of beauty, a sunset, a song, a child’s laugh. They talk about the things they paid attention to. No one says, on their deathbed, “I wish I had spent more time looking at my phone.” No one says, “I wish I had checked my email more often.” They say, “I wish I had spent more time with my family.” “I wish I had told her I loved her.” “I wish I had slowed down.” These are all statements about attention. To love someone is to pay attention to them. To regret not loving someone is to regret not paying attention to them. The end of life is a great clarifier. It strips away the noise. It reveals what was always important. But we do not have to wait until the end to know this. We can know it now. We can choose, every day, to stretch ourselves toward what matters.

I am back in the café, the coffee cold, the sun lower in the sky. The couple at the next table has stopped arguing. They are holding hands, silently. The barista has turned on some music, something slow and acoustic. Outside, people walk by with their heads down, their faces lit by the pale glow of screens. Inside, I am writing to you, and you are reading this, and in some strange way we are paying attention to each other across the void of time and space. This is a miracle, if you think about it. Language, moving from mind to mind, surviving the distance, evoking images and feelings in a brain that is not my own. That is all any of us can do: to reach out, to attend, to make something that another soul can hold. The essay is almost done. It has wandered, as I promised it would. But maybe it has not wandered aimlessly. Maybe it has been circling a single point, the way a hawk circles a field. The point is this: attention is the thread that connects us to everything. It is the substance of love, the medium of art, the engine of understanding. Guard it. Use it. Spend it on things that deserve it. And when you find yourself lost in the noise, come back to the simplest act: look at something, really look, and let it be enough.
